lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: I now call this meeting to order. Welcome here, everyone. Thank you for coming to the meeting. And at this time, I would like to give the opening to Councillor Jac Siemens.

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor
lines.label: Jac Siemens (Councillor)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. It's been almost 20 years. Matter of fact, almost 5 completed terms that I've sat here in this chair as a councillor for the City of Steinbach. Initially, the plan was 2 terms and done. I did my time, but it's turned out very different. A little bit of context. In 2006, the population of Steinbach was just over 11,000 people. Today, 22,000. Now think about that. In 20 years from now, in 2046, we could have, using those same numbers, 44,000 people living in Steinbach. In 2006, Steinbach was 25.6 square kilometres in size. Today, after the 2018 annexation, it is almost 38 square kilometres in size. In 2006, we had 133 kilometres of roadways to maintain. Today, it's over 145 kilometres. The budget for the City of Steinbach in 2006 was $29 million. There was a huge capital year that year. Today, You're going to hear it's $49 million. In 2006, Steinbach had 5 signalized intersections. Today, there are 13, plus one more coming on this year. If, if that's a sign of growth, not necessarily a positive one. In 2006, we had just over 5,200 private dwelling units. Today, there's over 7,500, which means we built an average of 115 private dwelling units each year for the past 20 years. Today we have 2.6 people per dwelling unit. That is up from 2006 when it was 2.17. Maybe our children are staying living with the parents longer now than they did 20 years ago. Looking back, it's been an interesting 20 years with many decisions that have affected how Steinbach has grown. Major changes in our thought process, like adding the CBD, or Central Business District, change how we see our downtown. Or even the friendly annexation of 2,800 acres from the Arm of Hanover in 2018, but it did secure land development for Steinbach for the next 40 to 50 years. But back to my time on council, here are a few lessons that I've learned. Learning the difference between management and governance. In my work life, I worked as a general manager, as an operations manager, as a customer service manager, always managing people, and process. As a councillor, we are directed to manage the governance of the city with our one employee, the city manager. Day-to-day operations are left in his hands, and council oversees the direction and policies of the city. We don't direct except to one employee. How much power I don't have as a councillor. You know, I have many great ideas. But they are useless if I can't convince at least a few councillors of how good an idea they are. It is a true team effort to get things completed as a city. While council doesn't always agree with the ideas or decisions made, we are still a team and address each other on the issue, not on our differences in our personalities. Understanding the language of variations, zoning, community plan, the various acronyms, bylaws, and how they all relate and work together for a comprehensive comprehensive plan that council approves and staff have to work with. The language is different. Learning that at each council meeting, someone might not leave happy because they've applied for a variation or some other thing, but another attendee will leave happy. While council generally makes the right decisions, we are not here to make everyone happy, as we do have to work within the policy guidelines that we have created. How to make a decision with information present in the form of council material. I still, after reading all the material handed out, I still have to do my own homework on the issue by talking to the people affected. What I've often struggled with is how do I listen? Do I listen to the loud minority, or how do I listen to the quiet majority? Knowing that each word is recorded, I need to be careful with words so as to be clear on the message I want to present. Not only are people listening online, the press is present at each meeting. How I would like to be heard and understood becomes part of how I prepare for each meeting. Looking back, I want some of my decisions back. On my second council meeting in 2006, we heard a request to split a large corner lot. I didn't think it was a good idea, but the recommendation from administration was to approve, plus previous council had approved a number of them in the prior term. While I didn't think it was a good idea, I was afraid or reluctant to speak to the issue and kept quiet with my opinion, and the request was approved. I drive by that corner frequently when council's faced with a difficult decision. It reminds me that I need to add my voice to the discussion. By the way, council has not approved a single splitting of a corner lot since that decision. My lessons have been learned along the way, and those are just a few. October 28th, Steinbach will elect a new city council again for another 4-year term. It is important for new faces and new ideas to sit at this table, and I would encourage anyone who wants to be involved to ask the questions of current or past council members of how they too can serve Steinbach as a councillor. Nominations for council will be accepted between September 16th and 22nd here at City Hall. While it sounds like there's a lot of time to contemplate running in the election, it is important to start thinking about being part of council today and, and what you think is important for you to bring to the table and continue to make Steinbach a great place to live, to raise a family, to work, to worship, and of course to ride a bike. Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Brian Hrehirchuk
lines.title: Senior Manager, Finance
lines.label: Brian Hrehirchuk (Senior Manager, Finance)
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor, members of council. I'm pleased to be presenting the city's 2026 financial plan to highlight some of the main items that are planned for the upcoming year. The annual budget cycle is almost a continuous process. For the 2026 year, it started early in 2025. Throughout the process, input is provided by staff, management, and council. The financial plan being presented today is based on the recommendations of council provided at their final review in November.

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Brian Hrehirchuk
lines.title: Senior Manager, Finance
lines.label: Brian Hrehirchuk (Senior Manager, Finance)
lines.text: Some of the highlights for 2026 include a municipal mill rate of 14.4 mills, which remains the same as 2025. Utility rates will increase by an average of 3%, while residential garbage collection rates will increase by 3.7%. Fees for permits are up 5%, and land use application fees will increase by 2.5%. The overall capital program for 2026 is budgeted at $35.8 million. Some of the larger budgeted projects include the Millwork Drive sewer replacement, Park Road West force main twinning, and Lift Station 1 upgrade. Overall, projected revenues for 2026 are just under $44 million. Similar to other years, property taxes are the city's largest source of revenue, accounting for just over half of the overall revenue amount. For 2026, there was a property value growth of 2.4%. Commercial properties continue to make up about 24% of total property values in the city, and with the provincial portioning system, a lower portion of residential property values are subject to property tax than commercial property values. As I mentioned earlier, the property tax rate of 14.4 mills is unchanged from 2025. 53% of budgeted municipal revenues are from property taxes, with $23.4 million to be raised by property taxes in 2026. The city is also required to collect the education and school taxes on behalf of the province and Hanover School Division. As in previous years, this is projected to make up roughly half of the total tax revenue collected by the city. The average market value for a dwelling in Steinbach is roughly $250,000. Based on this and the budgeted municipal mill rate, The average city property tax bill works out to roughly $135 per month. In addition to regular property taxes, supplementary property taxes are levied on new construction or where there was an additional improvement to increase the value of the property. This is expected to provide an additional $730,000 in 2026. Federal and provincial operating grants have also been a consistent source of revenue for the city. The provincial per capita tax sharing grant is expected to provide $4.8 million in 2026, while the federal gas tax grant will provide just over $1 million. One of the main non-tax revenues for the city is from user fees. These are fees paid by those who benefit from the service provided. Some services compete with the open market, but a number of these rates may be subsidized for programs to be accessible. Development in Steinbach stayed strong in 2025 with $118 million in total permit values. This activity is expected to continue into 2026 and beyond. Now we will look at some of the programs that are funded by these revenues. Overall, the expenses are equal to the projected revenues at just under $44 million. Some 2026 programs include waste reduction and recycling at just over $1.16 million, Support for the Jake Epp Public Library at $515,000, the beautification program at $300,000, and various other programs as listed. Every year, the city provides grants for various organizations throughout the city. In 2026, these grants total just over $1.1 million With the recipients as listed. One of the largest city expenses is that of our employees. The total labour cost, including benefits for 2026, is budgeted at $12.8 million, or just under a third of the city's operating budget. Of this total, the aquatic centre makes up about 18% of the total labour hours for The largest of any city department. Protective Services includes 18 RCMP officers, 53 firefighters and 8 fire trucks, as well as community services officers to enforce city bylaws. Protective— the total cost of these services is budgeted at $5.9 million for the upcoming year. The city currently has over 147 kilometers of road surface. The maintenance for this infrastructure can depend significantly on the weather in any given year, and for 2026 is expected to cost $3.4 million. Solid waste services. We provide both curbside and on-demand pickup services. to both residential and commercial properties. The cost of providing these services is expected to reach $3.4 million for the upcoming year, which is funded by user fees. Our primary recreation facilities include the Event Centre, Aquatic Centre, A.D. Penner Park, curling rink, and soccer park, as well as various green space and parks around the city. The expected cost of operating and maintaining these facilities is budgeted at $6.2 million for 2026. Both the number of customers serviced by the water and wastewater utility and the length of the underground infrastructure network continue to grow. The expected cost to maintain this infrastructure and provide the utility services is expected to be $4.8 million in 2026. In addition to the typical operating expenses that the city regularly incurs, larger projects also require significant funding. Some of this comes from reserve funds that have been saved in previous years, while other projects will require debt funding. Some of the main projects for the upcoming year include equipment replacement, the Park Road West force main twinning, and the Millwork Drive sewer renewal. The total capital program for the year is expected to be just under $36 million. I will now pass it over to Troy to expand on some of the items related to floodwater mitigation that are part of the financial plan.

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: Thank you. And for members of council and the public, there— we felt it was appropriate to do a bit of a segue in this presentation just to highlight some of the particular policies and initiatives that have been proposed with respect to, or in response to, a significant flooding event that affected the city in the fall of 2025, and which actually followed an event that affected the city in the fall of 2024. And in response to that, to that rainstorm event, council since that time, since September of last year, directed administration to investigate the event, identify opportunities for possible improvement, and prepare a detailed flood mitigation plan that could address areas within the city that were at a higher relative risk during storm events and to identify ways that the city and its infrastructure could become more resilient. So before I begin with, with 2026, I just wanted to highlight some of the initiatives that were undertaken in 2025, and that was since about the middle of September prior to the, the storm event and as part of the city's 2025 budgeting process.

lines.speaker: Michael Zwaagstra

lines.label: Michael Zwaagstra (Councillor)

lines.speaker: Troy Warkentin
lines.title: City Manager
lines.label: Troy Warkentin (City Manager)
lines.text: The city had already identified several projects and initiatives that it felt were important to address the ongoing growth of the city and also ongoing mitigation of possible risks that the city felt were reasonable to put forward. Council in the 2025 budget had approved a climate risk assessment study to be undertaken. That project did get underway in the summer of 2025. There was a smaller project to deal with drainage in the Clear Spring Greens neighborhood. It was fairly small by way of capital projects, but it was a way to try and increase the drainage capacity of the Clear Spring Greens neighborhood, and that total cost was approximately $30,000. There is an annual program for many services throughout the city that the city has undertaken for many years, and that is included in the city's sanitary sewer televising and maintenance program of an amount of just over $100,000 a year, its storm sewer televising and maintenance program of about $60,000 a year, And the city also undertakes a major drain maintenance program and allocates $50,000 a year to that program. In particular response to the fall storm event of 2025, the city did initiate working with Manitoba Disaster Financial Assistance and the province of Manitoba. to coordinate with affected homeowners. Unfortunately, after a review of that program, the Province of Manitoba had determined that a program would not be approved for Steinbach. And in late January, City Council did ask administration to follow up with that office. To date, we have not yet received a full We don't have a full response, but we do expect to have a report available for council within the next 2 to 4 weeks in response to that. As a result of the storm, administration also worked to determine a storm damage mapping program so that there would be a specific history of affected properties, which would help in the city's evaluation of what programs could be determined and proposed for the coming years. The city also undertook a significant cleanout program for the Keating Drain from PTH 52 West north to Park Road West. And I am pleased to say that that program, at a cost of about $30,000, was completed by November of last year. And finally, Administration, through working with its operating departments, coordinated with its waterworks department and recalibrated the operation of both its lift stations and water treatment plant so that any pumping capacity that is present in the system was able to operate at maximum effectiveness and capacity when storm events Moving forward and in what's proposed for the 2026 year, again, prior to the storm events occurring in both 2024 and 2025, City Council had directed administration to place 3 significant projects on its long-term capital plan. And those were already on that plan beginning in 2022. Thank you.

That proposed project will see essentially the doubling of pumping capacity of that lift station when that project is completed. The tender for that particular project actually is on council's agenda for consideration later on tonight. All totaled, those projects are in the neighborhood of about $8 to $9 million in total spending. That the city has or will consider awarding by tonight to be initiated in 2026. In addition, some projects that city council has directed administration to place in the budget for construction or to be addressed later on this year. Would be a program to further improve drainage along PTH 52 East, to undertake a further project to improve drainage along Park Road East in Steinbach. Through discussion and analysis, and as was presented at committee to council last week, Administration also recommended that council initiate a review of its sump pump bylaw 1674, along with a program to initiate the inspection and possible remediation of private property sewer, sump pit, and septic tank installations as a way to, first of all, inspect and verify the configurations that are present on private property and to research ways to improve those systems so that when storm events occur, that there is not any undue effluent being pumped into the city's sewer system. And finally, recommendation from City Council was for administration to review a project to reroute the low-pressure sewer line that is currently Servicing the Clear Spring Greens subdivision and reroute that line so that it would, rather than discharging into the Golfview Crescent sewer line, that that low-pressure sewer main would discharge into the park— sorry, PTH 12 North sewer line at the city's north end.

There was other projects related to a master plan for the city's drainage catchment areas, a review of the city's basement depth policy, particularly for new construction. There was a concept plan to investigate a possible major drain bypass or water detention plan, and also a program to install stormwater flow sensors at various points throughout the city and its sanitary sewer system. As I mentioned, in 2025 and 2026, there are several major capital projects that are intended to be undertaken Shortly, and the city continues to, to look at what other opportunities are there to try and reduce the overall risks to the city's infrastructure and to private property when storm events occur. lines.label: Brian Hrehirchuk (Senior Manager, Finance)
lines.text: The city will periodically issue debt in order to add or renew various infrastructure or facilities throughout the city. Each loan will fund a specific project. In 2026, 3 projects have a debt component. The event centre completion, the fire department ladder truck, and the force main twinning. This is expected to create $7.25 million of new debt, while $3.4 million of previously issued debt will be paid off. The city continues to use a 5-year amortization term for all of its debt, allowing us to borrow at lower interest rates than if a longer term was used. Our average interest rate for 2026 is just over 4%, while the debt balance at the end of the year is expected to be $16.7 million. Payments that are required for previously issued debt will total $3.9 million in 2026. Of this amount, $556,000 is interest. Funding for these debt payments is raised through property taxation, and for 2026, 2.427 mills will be required to raise the necessary funds. This equates to just under 17% of the total city tax rate. And finally, a longer-term overview of some of the expected requirements in future years. The 2026 program, as mentioned, is currently budgeted at $35.8 million, which includes infrastructure renewal, the force main twinning, and Millwork Drive sewer replacement. Beyond that, programs of $17.8 million, $58.3 million, and $45.6 million are currently estimated for the following 3 years. That concludes the presentation of the 2026 financial plan. Thank you, members of council. If there are any questions, I can answer them now.

And this is a budget that delivers on that promise. It was a very tough time year after year, one year apart, less than a few days of one year apart. And that wreaked havoc on our community and people in our community. And, Council, we were serious and we were committed. And I'm looking forward to these floodwater mitigation projects that we're doing. And I know the one is just— the one's still pending, but it's in the budget. The money for it's in the budget. So anyone here Is there anyone here with comments, questions, or objections to this file? I'll ask again. Is there anyone here with comments, questions, or objections to this file? Okay. lines.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mayor. This is a budget that I am pleased to motion forward as I feel it is a representation of our values and priorities as a community. It is a balance of tried and true wise fiscal responsibility as well as investment into the future. This is a budget for our kids, for the working families, and for seniors aging at home. It's a budget for families. This year, we will be working with a revenue budget of just shy of $44 million, funded with no tax change from last year's mill rate of 14.4 mills, keeping the taxation on each property the same as it was last year. With this combination of our $44 million revenue budget, reserves, and grant funding, we will be investing over $35 million in infrastructure, equipment replacement, and new builds. Infrastructure renewal has always been one of this council's main priorities, and this budget reflects that with $7.5 million in equipment renewal at the landfill, as well as a new ladder truck for our fire department. We will continue our asphalt renewal program through a significant investment in the Stone Bridge Crossing neighborhood with an additional $2.2 million budgeted for roadwork. And the largest focus in this budget is the renewal of our wastewater system, with over $20 million budgeted for wastewater renewal and new infrastructure. All of this is made possible because of long-term planning, aggressive tendering, and responsible debt management of this and previous councils. Even though we just undertook the largest infrastructure project in the city's history with the Southeast Event Centre, we are still holding true to our pledge of not taking debts for longer than a 5-year debenture. And while there is over $35 million of new infrastructure projects being funded this year, only $7.25 million is being taken out in debt, while $3.4 million is being retired for a very manageable and modest increase in our debt load. This strategy of keeping debt low and paying it off in only 5 years has made Steinbach the envy of many cities across Canada. And when we talk to our fellow peers across the nation, Without fail, we see jaws drop when we discuss that this is how Steinbach funds their projects, as this is not normal practice. But in my opinion, it is the best practice. Council also looked at the extreme rain events and the profound impact it has had in our residents and enacted a flood mitigation— water mitigation plan. Floodwater prevention infrastructure has had budget lines in our budget in the past. Some long-term and some that arise that need to be expedited, but this formalized a plan. Immediately after the latest event in September 2025, council and administration worked with the various departments to do some quick projects like cleaning our drains, calibrating the lift stations and treatment plant pumps for optimized flow, and mapping storm damage to look for solutions. This budget reflects investments in projects that were planned and waiting for additional funding such as the Lift Station 1 pumping capacity upgrades, as well as sewer capacity upgrades and improvements. Additional projects have been invested into, such as drainage improvements, various programs and reviews to reduce, reduce stormwater penetration into our sewer systems, and potential rerouting of force mains to connect more directly to our lift stations rather than routing them through other neighborhoods. I would like to thank every councillor for their hard work on preparing this. And for administration for their diligent work in balancing necessary projects while keeping the taxpayer in mind. In fact, through administration's work on early tendering project management, we are technically already under budget on many of the tendered projects, which will allow more funds to be directed towards reserves and future projects. This is a zero tax increase budget that invests into our city for our future. and the future of our children to make this a community that will be sustainable for generations.

It is 5 pages long, so I won't go through it in depth, but I would like to highlight Article 9 in it, which I will read in its entirety. And then I would like to read the first part of Article 10, and I'd like to read the concluding paragraph. Article 9 reads, the owner Hereby covenants and agrees— and I'll just stop at the word covenant. I looked it up in the Webster's Dictionary. Covenant means more than a contract. It means a solemn promise. The owner hereby covenants and agrees that the most northwesterly 190.9 feet in depth of Lot Block 2, Plan 10121 in the Town of Steinbach shall not be used for access to the site or for parking or for any other use ancillary to the development on the site other than as green space. And I'll leave it at that. I could go on Article 10, but I think it's quite clear, and I'd like to underline maybe any attempt to impeach the validity of this agreement. And then the concluding paragraph. It is understood that the covenants herein contained shall run with the land. And this agreement will be registered by way of caveat against the owner-owned lands so that all future owners of the land will have knowledge thereof and will be bound by the terms thereof. Signed by, again, the mayor and the housing corporation chair. When Councillor Reimer brought me this document, I was relieved. We could now go ahead and make a bid for this purchase. I asked [name withheld], who was a real estate agent at that time, to come and evaluate the property. And he said the price that [names withheld] were asking was a bit on the high side. We'd be paying a premium for it. But if we were crazy enough Go for it. Well, we were. We loved that house and that property, and we bought it, I think, for $90,000. We moved to Steinbach. We integrated into Steinbach. [name withheld] and [Resident 3] attended Elmdale School. Our son [name withheld] was in grade 1. [name withheld] taught piano in that house. She was a member of the Steinbach Arts Council. I got involved, we began attending Steinbach Mennonite Church. lines.speaker: Resident 2

lines.speaker: Resident 2

It loves taking care of its citizens. And there is a core that'll rise. And as a family, we would love to see this green space turn into what it could be. And that is a marquee park for the people who live on the west side of Main Street. Lots of green space on the east side. And to have children here in play structure and elderly people on park benches and trees planted. They say the best time to plant a tree is 25 years ago, or maybe 1989. Maybe the second best is this spring. And we would love to enter into a friendly discussion with Housing Corporation to see that happen. And recognizing that this is a progressive town and things will Change. But let's not make one of the things a green space set aside a generation ago by forward-thinking council members that every self-respecting city, right? You got Central Park in New York, you got Hyde Park in Chicago. We need green spaces and we need really marquee parks. And again, we would love to work with Steinbach Housing.

lines.speaker: Michael Obviar

lines.speaker: Resident 2
lines.label: Resident 2

lines.speaker: Resident 3

We don't normally do this. Normally we'll make the decision right, right now because that's the ideal way to do it. lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. I don't agree with the motion at all. I think that we can make a decision. The parking issue is confusing and it should have been dealt with before this meeting. Not—

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: It shouldn't—

lines.speaker: Jac Siemens
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: We shouldn't delay the hearing because of the parking issue. It's confusing, and I could speak to the parking issue, but that's not what's important. What's important is the bylaw 1171 from 1989. There is a caveat there. Council of the day did make a decision, and that was part of the decision. That was also part of the requirement at that time. When you built Lindenwood— Linden Place, they had to set aside X amount of green space. That was part of the agreement. I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. And we need to honour that agreement. And to simply say no, that's no longer it because we've changed, it's transitional zone now, so that doesn't take care— we still have to have a motion of council, I'd assume, to eliminate that caveat at some point. And, or maybe, maybe we even have to go to a public hearing. I'm ready to make a decision on this, but I, but I respect the fact— I think this is maybe the 3rd time in 20 years that we have delayed a Council decision because of a request to move it to another meeting. We don't have enough information. It's not council's fault there's not enough information that it's confusing to us. That's not our issue. That is on the— that goes on the applicant. For me, Friesen Avenue is a whole lot of single-family homes. This disrupts it. C-1 allows up to 3 levels, not 7. And so I think our biggest issue downtown now, we've talked about this period, is large single-family homes, large lots, single-family homes. What do you do with them? You can't— a lot of the people don't want to build a single-family home on those large lots. It's too expensive. And it's not the place. Downtown, at some point, as these neighbourhoods transition, are going to be more multifamily. We've seen that. They cobble together They gather a couple of these lots and they put in multifamily. I agree with all that, and I agree that we need more seniors housing. I know people who are on the list at Fernwood and at Linden Place, and I don't agree with the parking discussion. Fernwood Place, when I go see people at Fernwood Place, I park on the street because there's nothing there. And when I talk to the people who live there, they struggle. They want parking, but they want indoor parking. Which is different from the other parking that they all have. So there's a lot of struggles, but I would have hoped the applicant would become more prepared in the first place so that we could make a decision today so that we don't have to make a decision down the road. I would have preferred to make the decision today. Therefore, I'll vote against the motion.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor

lines.speaker: Jake Hiebert
lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: No, no, yeah, all I'm asking is for a footprint of the building. I'm not asking for a total design of the building, just a footprint, because that would direct us then where the parking would be. Just make it clarified a little more. That's all I was asking.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: We do have a site plan though here.

lines.speaker: Michael Obviar
lines.title: Director of Housing

lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor

lines.title: Councillor

lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor. Just a couple of things in response, and I do appreciate Councillor Siemens' for those comments and keeping us on our toes on some of this. I agree the parking is confusing. That's why I want more information. And I think there is potential here that it's possible that something here might work. And I don't want to dismiss the possibility of a project of this nature and this importance because we don't have all the information and because we know that we could— we can get more of the information. And this is our staff recommendation. adjourning. But this is actually something our staff recommended, and after hearing what was here today, the parking is the main issue that, that I'm noticing, and I would like to get more info on that. In response to Councillor Siemens, as far as the agreement from 1989, as with every agreement, it is binding so long as both parties are in agreement with it. So there's nothing in here that is being broken as far as, like, the— it says the owner hereby covenants and agrees. I'm not saying that. Of course, because— but it's the town or the city now. Obviously, if both parties agree to make a change, a change could be made. Now, whether we will make that change is going to largely hinge on the information that we get presented to us subsequently in regards to some of the parking and some of the other things. But when both sides agree on a change, that's when agreements can change. I mean, this is— that is not terribly unusual. I mean, one of the basic things in law is that— I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. If any contract can be changed, if both parties that have signed the contract agree to change it. I mean, that's just basic law. So, but as far as whether we remove the caveat is largely going to depend on what decision we make in regards to the variances and the other thing here, and we will get some of the additional info and then we'll decide at that point.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: Thank you very much. Okay, Council, I just want to start with thank you very much for what you do in our community.

lines.speaker: Brian Hrehirchuk

lines.label: Unidentified speaker
lines.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayor.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor

lines.text: I appreciate your time.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor) [medium]
lines.text: I appreciate your commitment to the community, and senior housing is, is definitely needed.

lines.speaker: Earl Funk
lines.title: Mayor
lines.label: Earl Funk (Mayor)
lines.text: You do a great job of it, and you do— your aging in place is, is, is just second to none. But thank you for agreeing to go back, getting some more information for us so we can make this, this decision. Council, we don't do this. We normally don't table a subject and bring it back. But that doesn't mean it's not— it's a good thing. In this case, I think it's good for further clarity so that we know what to do. I think I agree with Councillor Susan Penner. Looking at this agreement a little bit in more depth would be a good idea for council to do. I think we should do that. I was thinking very much along the lines of Councillor Zwaagstra. That yes, agreements can be changed as long as both parties agree to change. But I do want to look at this, unwrap this agreement together with council, and I think that if we have more information at a later date, which will be April 21st, at that time we will make decisions on both of these situations.

lines.speaker: Michael Obviar
